extra.summary: Long neglected and marginalized by the state, inhabitants of Turkey’s southeast region, particularly its Kurdish communities, look not to the official courts but to renowned local figures, religious leaders, and civil organizations to resolve disputes. This paper explores three types of alternative judicial bodies (AJBs): (1) traditional Heqî AJBs, which prioritize religion and patriarchy in their decision-making; (2) self-identified progressive AJBs run by local civil society organizations; and (3) newly emerging AJBs aligned with state institutions, reflecting the state’s new frontiers in the region. Although these judicial bodies, shaped by diverse adjudicative tendencies and deeply embedded in the region’s religious, political, and social fabric, differ in their impact in terms of whom and what they include or exclude, they collectively provide alternative pathways for dispute resolution. This paper examines the role of AJBs in resolving disputes in the Kurdish southeast, focusing on gender, religious discourses, the involvement of feminist activists and organizations, and the positionality of these bodies within regional politics and sovereignty formation. Based on ethnographic fieldwork in Mardin, it examines interactions between Kurdish AJBs and women’s agency and mobility, while situating AJBs within broader debates on legal pluralism and gender justice in feminist legal scholarship.

items.title: The Diaspora of Pre-Columbian Objects from Atacama into a Global Network of Goods, Collectors, and Museums between 1850 and 1950

extra.summary: Pre-Columbian objects from Atacama not only held value and articulated social relations in pre-European times. To this day, and from at least the nineteenth century onward, they continue to play this role by being exhibited in national and international museum showcases, reproduced in catalogs, or owned by private collectors. It is clear that their past value was changed in these new contexts, but what did not change was their amazing ability to bring individuals and institutions together across time and space, even across continents and generations. The bonds forged in the acquisition, circulation, and possession of these ancient objects and collections formed a global network of relationships between humans and things. Such a web was not woven randomly or whimsically but rather warped within the structure of the world system where the Atacama Desert has participated since the mid-nineteenth century, orchestrated principally by the saltpeter, copper, industrial, and mercantile economies. The circulation and biographies of pre-Columbian objects from Atacama is an extraordinary source for understanding the world system in which they were extracted, exchanged, accumulated, assembled, inherited, and exhibited between 1850 and 1950. This dual reflection also opens up a fantastic possibility to better comprehend the role of the cultural works of the past in the making of each social reality at different moments in time.

items.title: An Archaeology of Redress

extra.summary: Black studies critical theorizations have much to offer the field of archaeology both in theory and in practice. For Saidiya Hartman, redress entails confronting formations of epistemic violence that undergird the archival record; it is a praxis that is always incomplete. This article maps Hartman’s theory of redress onto the practice of community archaeology to explore the opportunities and challenges that arise when archaeologists center youth engagement, capacity building, and cultural and natural heritage stewardship. Using the Estate Little Princess Archaeology Project as a case study, we explore one way archaeologists attempt to offer restitution to the issues their work reveals (i.e., legacies of environmental racism, truncated avenues of economic sustainability, racialized disenfranchisement) through an “archaeology of redress.”

items.title: Interracial Publics

extra.summary: This article examines the formation of “interracial publics” in postapartheid South Africa, showing how race, intimacy, and belonging are negotiated through mediated encounters. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, interviews, and media analysis, it traces how relationships between people historically classified as “white” and “nonwhite” become publicly visible and collectively interpreted across print, broadcast, and digital platforms. These publics are ambivalent and contested: they can normalize formerly forbidden intimacies and foster cross-racial connection, yet they also reinscribe racialized hierarchies through gendered and sexualized discourse. Situating these dynamics within South Africa’s longer histories of settler colonialism and apartheid, the article argues that the regulation of intimacy has been central to projects of racial governance and white supremacy and continues to animate their afterlives in contemporary struggles over visibility, belonging, and desire. Interracial intimacy functions as both a measure and a mediator of contemporary racial formations, contributing to comparative anthropological debates on race, media, affect, and the public sphere in postcolonial societies.

extra.summary: Drawing on recent critiques of liberal conceptions of legal-juridical citizenship, this article develops a model of disenchanted citizenship that moves away from treating legal-juridical citizenship as an unqualified good, normative value, or universal concept. Building on the concept of the regionally specific citizenship regime, constructions of citizenship that can be bound within one nation-state or extend across several, the article examines the inequalities, instabilities, and exclusions that remain central to contemporary regional constructions of citizenship. By offering new language to describe old and new processes of de-documentation, the review and revocation of core identity documents, and de-citizenship, the revocation of birthright or naturalized citizenship, the essay explores how citizenship remains a site of bio-documentary power, the power to make and unmake populations through the production, interrogation, destabilization, and even destruction of digital and physical files and documents.

items.title: A closer look at the postcranial skeleton of Omo I from the Kibish Formation, Ethiopia: points of divergence from recent humans
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Previous studies have described the postcranial skeleton of Omo I as anatomically modern yet have often noted features in its anatomy that are unusual in comparison to recent humans. The present study presents an analysis of linear measurements of many portions of the skeleton in comparison to several samples of recent (Holocene) humans. Special attention is paid to contrasts with Zulu males, a sample that approximates Omo I in overall size. The results show that Omo I has a long humerus with a slender shaft, a proximally positioned ulnar tuberosity, a short olecranon process, large articular ends and flattened proximal articular surface of the first metacarpal, a large acetabulum, a narrow patellar notch, and a low talus with a long neck. These join the set of distinctive features identified in previous analyses and combine to push the skeleton away from recent humans in multivariate space. A few of the features appear to be plesiomorphic, others apomorphic and ‘modern’, and some possibly idiosyncratic. Close inspection of the unusual dimensions suggests that some are unreliable, including the original estimate for humeral length. This implies that Omo I had a stout rather than linear build.

items.title: Gough's Cave and biomolecular archaeology: a story of evolving interpretation
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: Gough's Cave is a key archaeological site that has been at heart of British archaeology for the past century. Professor Chris Stringer, whom this special issue honours, has been a key figure in excavations and research projects at the site for many decades. Here, I detail how the ever‐increasing weight of biomolecular data generation over the past 50 years, which includes radiocarbon dating, dietary isotope, and ancient DNA analysis, has resulted in an ever‐evolving interpretation of the two oldest and most archaeologically significant assemblages at the site: the Mesolithic skeleton of Cheddar Man (between 10,600 and 9,900 years ago), and the large post‐glacial deposit attributed to the Magdalenian culture (between 15,100 and 14,300 years ago).

items.title: Middle-class locations: emplacements and displacements of habitus among the French in London
items.affiliation: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

extra.summary: This article examines the alterations of habitus that lead to feelings of emplacement and displacement among middle-class French citizens living in London. I broaden Bourdieu’s concept of split habitus, developed primarily in the context of social mobility, and extend it to questions of geographic mobility. I characterize the French in London as “sideways migrants” who move to a nearby nation with comparable socio-economic indicators and global standing, seeking to maintain their middle-class status through transversal mobility. They are “nation straddlers” who experience dislocations of habitus shaped in the French national social space after relocating to London. I present the cases of four French women in London, drawing upon a larger longitudinal ethnographic study, to expand understandings of how migrant aspirations and practices are connected to the positionality of habitus in both the social space of the nation of origin and that of resettlement. Migration research that situates migrants in national social spaces that they straddle, as in the case of sideways migrants, has important implications for broader questions about the durability and nature of both class and national identity in the contemporary world.

items.title: Nationalism, Balance of Power, and World Order: Untangling Neorealism's Troubled Relationship With Nationalism

extra.summary: ABSTRACT While many explain the crisis of the liberal international order through nationalism, its treatment by neorealist scholars remains frustrating. Untangling the nationalism–neorealism relationship would help explain the current crisis and enhance neorealism's explanatory power. First, this article reviews and critically assesses neorealist scholarship (defensive, offensive and neoclassical realism) about nationalism. Then, using these insights, I propose a distinctively neorealist theory of nationalism. International power shifts reshape nationalism, which, in turn, conditions the behaviour and discourse of the great powers. Rising material capabilities foster offensive nationalism; diminishing capabilities foster defensive nationalism. Hence, global power shifts—foremost the United States' decline relative to China and Russia—transformed the great powers' nationalism, breaking the post‐Cold War order. This approach enables predictions about nationalism's future. If the global power distribution stabilises, the ‘distribution’ of nationalism should stabilise, too; the evolution of nationalism shows a degree of predictability. Pursuing a ‘neorealist nationalism’ research agenda helps tackle fundamental questions about the international order.

items.title: Affective boundaries: a computational analysis of topic dynamics and sentiment in online reactions to Seoul's Filipino domestic worker pilot programme
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
items.affiliation: Nanjing University; Yonsei University; National Chengchi University; University of Hong Kong

extra.summary: In 2024, the Seoul Metropolitan Government launched the Foreign Housekeeping Managers Pilot Project, employing Filipino domestic workers to address care labour shortages amid low fertility and aging. As Korea's first formal institutionalisation of migrant care work, it offers a rare chance to observe how public commenters on Naver, the country's dominant news portal, interpret and contest this change. Using a mixed-methods computational approach combining manual topic classification, LDA topic modelling, and deep learning-based sentiment analysis, we analyse 543 news articles and 20,685 comments from September 2024 to April 2025. Seven themes appeared: working conditions and wages, policy rollout, public reactions, international comparisons, migrant rights concerns, the programme as a response to care shortages and fertility decline, and alternative models. Sentiment skewed heavily negative, dominated by anger and disgust tied to perceived unfairness and contested belonging. Fluctuations tracked policy events, showing how administrative developments became political flashpoints. We use the concept of affective boundary-making, advanced as a synthesis of symbolic boundary work and affective publics rather than as a new theoretical construct, to describe how anger and disgust function as the medium through which deservingness boundaries are drawn during the pre-institutional phase of a care-migration policy.

items.title: Infrastructure nationalism and sovereignty by settlement in Tibet: The case of xiaokang border villages

extra.summary: This article critically examines China’s Xiaokang Border Village Programme (2017–20) in the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), situating it within Xi Jinping’s broader strategy of ‘governing the borders to govern the country’. Ostensibly framed as a poverty alleviation and rural revitalization initiative, the programme mobilized billions in state funding to construct or rebuild more than 600 model villages in Tibet’s border counties. Drawing on a range of new sources, the article argues that these villages are less developmental tools than instruments of territorial consolidation, securitization, and ideological transformation. By reconfiguring spatial relations, relocating border populations, and embedding Han-led Chinese Communist Party (CCP) institutions, these xiaokang villages function as micro-sites of infrastructure nationalism and colonial-style governance, inscribing Han norms into Indigenous landscapes and subjectivities to further CCP control over once autonomous communities in the farthest reaches of the People’s Republic of China.

items.title: Globalizing the Tribal Culture, Landscapes and Customary Practices Through Indigenous Tourism
items.affiliation: Central Tribal University of Andhra Pradesh; Andhra Pradesh Forest Department

extra.summary: The world today is focusing on the concept of inclusivity and holistic development. The indigenous communities are at the edge of it to ensure the integrated growth of man and nature. They are critical for fostering well-being of humankind through sustainable practices. India is home to 104.2 million indigenous people of the world and the second largest indigenous territory after China. These indigenous people are rich in their rituals, customary practices and their age-old knowledge systems. They have passed on their knowledge from one generation to another for ages orally; however, lack of documentation has resulted in their cultural loss. It includes various cultural elements such as dance, music, painting, fairs, festivals, storytelling, puppetry and so on. Especially, in the era of globalization, when the cultural homogenization is taking place at a faster pace due to the effect of digitalization and modernization, the traditional artefacts of tribes are vanishing quickly. This research article thus tries to document various unique cultural footprints of tribes from different parts of the country. The article particularly focuses on the scope and role of indigenous tourism, which plays an important role in familiarizing various cultural regimes to tribal landscapes and enhances the process of glocalization, that is, global to local. This can further boost the tribal economy as well as acquaint tribal material culture to the world.

items.affiliation: Vietnam National University, Hanoi; The University of Sydney

extra.summary: While Community-Based Tourism (CBT) is widely championed for rural development, its capacity to deliver equitable empowerment remains heavily contested. This study empirically evaluates the multidimensional impacts of CBT across economic, social, cultural, and environmental dimensions in Northwest Vietnam, identifying the structural determinants of its sustainability impacts. Conversely, individual household capacities, ethnic attachment, and subsidised financial credit largely fail to produce sustainability outcomes. However, household livelihood resilience under protected-area land use restrictions is rarely explained by a single factor; rather, it is better understood through the combined configurations of spatial constraint intensity, natural-capital dependence, social capital, and alternative livelihood capacity. Taking households in five sampled Yi, Qiang, and Hui villages around the Giant Panda National Park in China as empirical cases, this study examines the configurational relationships through which land use restrictions are associated with household livelihood resilience. items.title: Spatial Relationships and Influencing Factors of Traditional Villages and Intangible Cultural Heritage in the Yunnan Section of the China–Vietnam Border

extra.summary: The prefectures and cities along the Yunnan–Vietnam border constitute a key cultural corridor connecting China and ASEAN. items.title: Climate Extremes, Demographic Restructuring, and Population Exposure in Xinjiang: Potential Socio-Cultural Implications in a Multi-Ethnic Arid Region
items.affiliation: Yunnan University; GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences

extra.summary: Extreme climate change and demographic change jointly reshape human exposure in arid and culturally diverse regions. This study examines projected changes in climate extremes and population exposure in Xinjiang, China, during 2021–2100 under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5–8.5 (SSP5-8.5). An ensemble of eight models from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) was used to assess very wet-day precipitation (R95p), warm days (TX90p), and consecutive dry days (CDD), while gridded total-population projections were combined with provincial-level age- and education-specific demographic projections. Comparing the late-century period (2081–2100) with the early-century baseline (2021–2040), ensemble-mean R95p increases by approximately 47%, TX90p by 167%, and CDD decreases by about 9.9%. Population remains concentrated in oasis cities and piedmont zones, with urbanization increasing from 49.6% to 77.0%. Demographic restructuring substantially changes the composition of exposure: the elderly share rises from 9.3% to 39.4%, producing the fastest increase in age-specific exposure, while the highly educated population expands from 5.5% to 48.6%. The reliability of the scale was assessed through internal consistency reliability, split-half reliability, and test–retest reliability. extra.summary: Against the backdrop of the concurrent processes of tourism development, spatial commercialisation, and architectural heritage conservation, identifying tourists’ cognitive images of destinations and differences in textual valence provides an important basis for evaluating the quality of tourism built environments and implementing fine-grained spatial governance. The results show that, under a theory-guided codebook, review content can be organised into four dimensions: natural landscapes, built heritage, ethnic culture, and services and accessibility. Natural mountain–lake scenery has the broadest review coverage, while strong semantic associations among architectural character, Bai vernacular dwellings, and Bai culture indicate that built heritage is an important spatial representation through which tourists recognise local culture. Textual valence is predominantly positive: positive, neutral, and negative affective terms account for 71.87%, 22.65%, and 5.48%, respectively. items.title: Ethnic narratives in Dunhuang Bianwen: a digital humanities approach to pluralistic integration

extra.summary: As a representative form of folk storytelling and singing literature in the Tang Dynasty, Dunhuang Bianwen emerged in the multi-ethnic borderland of northwest China. It directly reflects the perceptions of ethnic interactions in folk society and possesses significant research value. Guided by the ethnic boundary theory, this study takes the 78 Bianwen texts recorded in the Collected Works of Dunhuang Bianwen (Wang et al., 1957). It constructs a quantitative model integrating three core indicators—Interaction Density, Emotional Orientation, and Interaction Impact intensity—and Standard History Narrative Distance Coefficient, analyzing the interactions between the Han ethnic group and surrounding ethnic minorities including the Turks and Tibetans. This research reveals the narrative essence of “differences exist in interactions while connections are sustained through differences” within the pluralistic integration pattern of the Chinese nation, and offers an interdisciplinary analytical paradigm for relevant studies.

extra.summary: Purpose This study aims to establish a theoretical framework to explore the generation and evolution of Dai settlements in Xishuangbanna, Yunnan Province. The study of Dai settlements is essential for comprehending, preserving and developing the Dai ethnic cultural heritages amid rapid modernization. Design/methodology/approach This article examines the traditional villages in Xishuangbanna, Yunnan Province, China, with a focus on Dai settlements and dwellings from the 1980s to the present, employing a multidisciplinary approach consisting of theoretical analysis, field research and graphic interpretation. Findings This study investigates the material, spiritual and social dimensions that have shaped the formation and evolution of the Dai villages amid modernization. By analyzing two representative spatial cases, it illustrates that Dai villages emerged from a dynamic interplay among multiple dimensions, with varying degrees of impact at every stage. Originality/value This three-dimensional analytical framework offers a deeper understanding of rural settlements from both internal and external perspectives. It provides theoretical insights and practical guidance for architects, planners and policymakers engaged in cultural heritage conservation and rural revitalization.

items.title: Fluvial Dreams of Modernity: Hydropower Infrastructure, Global Networks, and State Making in Xikang, 1939–1947

extra.summary: Abstract : When China’s Republican government fled to Chongqing during the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), it brought with it a heightened demand for electricity production for the war effort. The relocation of the Nationalist government and an ambitious new generation of Chinese technocrats to Sichuan Province brought unprecedented resources to West China. After Xikang Province was formally established in 1939, the provincial government under Liu Wenhui acted as a key intermediary that connected the central government’s desire for wartime resources with Xikang elites and officials’ interest in local energy development projects. This new alignment of interests allowed the Xikang provincial government to secure the technical expertise, finances, and equipment necessary to build two state-of-the-art hydropower dams during the wartime period. The legacies of these projects and the engineering experts who worked on them were foundational to the earliest imaginings of the vast scale and potential of hydroelectricity in the Sino-Tibetan borderland.

items.title: The spatio-temporal pattern and influencing factors of toponymic cultural heritage in Ningxia
items.affiliation: Ocean University of China; Qingdao University; Chinese Academy of Sciences; Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research

extra.summary: Toponymic cultural heritage (TCH) forms a critical yet often undervalued layer of cultural landscapes, encapsulating historical human-environment interactions. Despite growing focus on heritage conservation, a significant research gap persists: there is limited empirical evidence on how TCH spatial clustering evolves across historical periods and what specific environmental and socio-demographic thresholds drive its concentration, hindering the development of temporally and spatially nuanced conservation strategies. Addressing this gap, this study analyzes the spatio-temporal patterns and drivers of TCH across 22 county-level units in Ningxia, China. Spatial autocorrelation analysis (Global Moran’s I) reveals significant positive spatial dependence with a pulsed pattern of alternating weak and strong agglomeration over time. Peak clustering occurred between the Qin-Han and Song-Yuan dynasties. The distribution is shaped by an interplay of natural and social factors; an optimal ‘moderate zone’ characterized by a relative height difference of 500–1000 m, a river network density of 50–150 m/km2, and a contemporary Hui population below 500,000 fosters the highest concentration of culturally significant toponyms. items.title: The green nexum: Collateral, clan finance and the moral economy of repo markets

extra.summary: This paper analyses the attempted greening of repurchase agreement (repo) markets through the figure of the ‘green nexum’. Repos are not green in themselves: collateral normally matters insofar as it is liquid, eligible and reusable. Drawing on critical macro-finance, social studies of finance and anthropological theories of exchange, the paper argues that repo markets are not neutral financial ‘plumbing’ but a Braudelian antimarket: an elite, state-entangled formation above ordinary market exchange. The circulation of collateral produces a distinct sociality, binding dealer banks, central banks and asset managers into ranked chains of obligation. Based on fieldwork in international industry standard-setting forums, green-finance training and interviews, the paper shows how green repo attempts to moralize, yet reproduces, collateral-based finance.
